article_title: Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review.
citation: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627
title: PjBL as a student-centred inquiry approach defined by key elements: driving problem, final product, group work, student empowerment, teacher guidance, and adapted evaluation tools
description: The review characterizes PjBL (used to cover both project- and problem-based learning) as "active, student-centred methods of instruction that encourage students to work in collaborative groups on real-world questions or challenges" with teachers as facilitators. Its central elements are a problem driving the activities, a final artifact or product, group work, student empowerment, teacher-provided guidance and resources, and evaluation tools adapted to PjBL such as notebook entries or portfolios. The review built a 30-item scale from these principles to assess prerequisites and fidelity.
requirements: An intervention faithful to the PjBL approach should include all its essential components as defined in the literature
constraints: PjBL and PBL are often employed interchangeably among researchers and teachers due to difficulties in distinguishing or defining their key features
examples: The review coded each included study against the key elements using a 30-item scale divided into prerequisites (Part A) and intervention fidelity (Part B)
key_sources: Ferrero Marta, Vadillo Miguel A., León Samuel P. (2021). Is project-based learning effective among kindergarten and elementary students? A systematic review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0249627

citation: Baker, Ryan S.J.d., Goldstein, Adam B., Heffernan, Neil T. (2011). Detecting Learning Moment-by-Moment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. In Press.
title: P(J): a two-step model assessing the probability a student just learned a KC at a specific problem step
description: P(J), short for 'Just Learned', is a machine-learned estimate of the probability that a student learned a knowledge component at a specific problem step, distinct from P(T) in standard Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. Training labels are generated using "a combination of predictions of current student knowledge from standard Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and data on future correctness, integrated using Bayes' Theorem"; the resulting model predicts P(J) at run time using only features of the current action, with no future data. It was instantiated as linear regression models with M5' feature selection for both the Cognitive Tutor and ASSISTments. The authors additionally derive a secondary 'spikiness' measure, the maximum value of P(J) for a student/KC pair divided by that pair's average P(J).
requirements: Training labels must be generated via Bayesian Knowledge Tracing estimates plus future correctness on two following steps before fitting the run-time model.
Feature sets (23 features for the Cognitive Tutor, 22 for ASSISTments) and log data labeled with knowledge components are needed to apply the modeling procedure.
constraints: The model tends to underestimate high values of P(J) in the training labels.
The learning window is biased toward post-answer processes: learning at step N is defined as occurring between the first answer on step N and the first answer on step N+1.
Model parameters are difficult to interpret individually because a feature's sign can flip depending on other parameters in the regression.
target_learners: Middle school and high school mathematics students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Moment-by-moment detection of knowledge component acquisition in mathematics
examples: Linear regression with M5' feature selection in RapidMiner, validated with 6-fold student-level cross-validation on both tutors' data
key_sources: Baker, Ryan S.J.d., Goldstein, Adam B., Heffernan, Neil T. (2011). Detecting Learning Moment-by-Moment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. In Press. https://doi.org/10.3233/JAI-2011-015

citation: Baker, Ryan S.J.d., Goldstein, Adam B., Heffernan, Neil T. (2011). Detecting Learning Moment-by-Moment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. In Press.
title: P(J) moment-of-learning feature sets for the Cognitive Tutor and ASSISTments
description: Two non-identical feature sets distilled from prior detectors of off-task behavior and gaming the system were used to predict P(J). The Cognitive Tutor used "23 features previously distilled to use in the development of contextual models of guessing and slipping", and ASSISTments used "a similar but non-identical list of 22 features", differing primarily due to the systems' different features and problem organization. Feature categories include correctness assessments, time measurements, hint usage, scaffolding usage (ASSISTments only), and other measurements such as whether the response was selected from a list or filled in, plus P(Ln-1) and P(Ln).
requirements: Transaction logs labeled with knowledge components so Bayesian Knowledge Tracing can be applied.
RapidMiner or equivalent for linear regression with M5' feature selection.
constraints: 290,698 Cognitive Tutor transactions were excluded from analyses because they were not labeled with KCs.
target_learners: Middle school and high school mathematics students using the Cognitive Tutor or ASSISTments
target_learning_goals: Predicting the probability of learning a knowledge component at a specific practice opportunity
examples: Tables 1 and 2 print the full regression equations for each system's P(J) model, including non-unitized parameter coefficients and constant terms
